context:
Patient: 67M with 6 wk epigastric/LUQ pain, drenching night sweats and 8 kg weight loss; ECOG 2, T2DM on metformin, taking ibuprofen 400 mg QID. PET-CT: 9.4 cm retroperitoneal/mesenteric mass plus FDG-avid R kidney, L adrenal and liver lesions; GCB DLBCL (MYC 20%, BCL2 30%, FISH negative), marrow negative, LDH 1,290, uric acid 10.4, creatinine 1.1 -> 1.5.
What this case tests: Kidney, adrenal and liver lesions are extranodal organ disease, so stage IV, IPI 5/5 and CNS-IPI 6/6. | MYC 20% / BCL2 30% with negative FISH: neither double-expressor nor double-hit, so no intensified regimen such as DA-EPOCH-R. | ECOG 2 is disease-related in a patient who wants cure: full-dose Pola-R-CHP (or R-CHOP) x6 after a steroid prephase, not mini-CHOP or palliation. | Uric acid 10.4, LDH >5x ULN and rising creatinine mean high TLS risk: IV hydration, rasburicase after G6PD check, TLS labs every 6-12 hours for the first 72 hours, stop NSAIDs. | High CNS risk: MRI brain and LP with CSF cytology/flow now; HD-MTX only as an individualized option once renal function recovers and NSAIDs are stopped.

answer.diagnosis:
Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma, NOS (DLBCL, NOS), germinal-center B-cell-like (GCB) subtype by the Hans algorithm, primary/de novo presentation, previously untreated.

Diagnostic basis (CT-guided core biopsy of the retroperitoneal mass, 2026-09-10, reported 2026-09-12, amended 2026-09-16): diffuse sheets of large atypical lymphoid cells with vesicular chromatin, prominent nucleoli, frequent mitoses and focal necrosis; no starry-sky pattern. IHC: CD20 diffuse strong positive, PAX5 positive, CD3 negative in tumor cells, CD5 negative, CD10 diffuse positive, BCL6 positive, MUM1/IRF4 negative (<10%), BCL2 positive in approximately 30% of cells, MYC positive in approximately 20%, cyclin D1 negative, CD30 negative, Ki-67 approximately 70%, EBER-ISH negative. Interphase FISH on block A1 (break-apart probes, 200 nuclei scored, adequate): NO rearrangement of MYC (8q24), BCL2 (18q21) or BCL6 (3q27).

Therapeutic consequences of the biology: this is NOT high-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC and/or BCL2 rearrangements, and it does NOT meet the immunohistochemical double-expressor definition (MYC 20% is below the 30-40% threshold; BCL2 30% is below the >=50% threshold used as a surrogate for t(14;18)). Therefore R-CHOP-based standard-dose curative therapy is appropriate, intensified high-grade B-cell-lymphoma regimens are not, and upfront consolidative autologous stem cell transplant in first remission is not indicated. Transformed DLBCL is excluded (no prior radiotherapy or chemotherapy). The panel also excludes CLL/SLL (CD5 negative), mantle cell lymphoma (cyclin D1 negative), PMBCL (CD30 negative) and T-cell or EBV-driven disease (CD3 negative, EBER negative).

Extranodal disease attribution: the right renal cortical lesion (3.2 cm, SUVmax 19.6), left adrenal mass (2.6 cm, SUVmax 17.2) and hepatic segment VI lesion (1.8 cm, SUVmax 15.0) are all intensely FDG-avid in a patient with biopsy-proven nodal DLBCL, and the avidity is far above what is typical for renal cell carcinoma; I am treating these as lymphoma and do not believe a separate biopsy of the renal lesion is required for management (it would not change systemic therapy and carries bleeding risk in a patient with CKD and planned thrombocytopenia). I will re-biopsy the renal lesion only if it behaves discordantly at restaging.

Residual diagnostic uncertainty that could change management: (a) high-grade B-cell lymphoma with 11q aberration, since this tumor is CD10+/BCL6+ GCB, EBV-negative, MYC/BCL2/BCL6-rearrangement-negative with a high Ki-67; (b) an MYC-rearrangement-negative Burkitt or Burkitt-like lymphoma (argued against by Ki-67 70% rather than >85-90%, absence of starry-sky morphology, and absence of MYC rearrangement); (c) the renal lesion as a second primary RCC with nodal metastases (argued against by the extreme FDG avidity and by biopsy-proven lymphoma in the contiguous nodal mass). I am ordering IG (IGH/IGK/IGL) rearrangement FISH with IGHD clonality and flow cytometry on the core, plus hematopathology re-review; if these show a high-grade B-cell lymphoma I will change to intensified therapy and plan autologous transplant in CR1. On the current record the diagnosis is DLBCL, NOS, GCB.
answer.stage:
Ann Arbor stage IV, B-symptomatic, with three extranodal organs involved.

Sites: right renal cortex, left adrenal gland, and liver segment VI (3 extranodal sites). Spleen uninvolved (11 cm, no focal uptake). Bone marrow uninvolved by PET and by aspirate/biopsy with flow cytometry (2026-09-13). No FDG-avid disease above the diaphragm (no mediastinal, hilar, axillary, cervical or supraclavicular nodes; no pleural effusions); no ascites; no hydronephrosis; no testicular involvement.

B symptoms: drenching night sweats most nights, unintentional weight loss from 79 kg to 70.2 kg (11%, 8.8 kg over about 2 months), low-grade fever to 37.9 C, and fatigue with reduced stamina.

Tumor bulk: conglomerate para-aortic and aortocaval plus mesenteric nodal mass measuring 9.4 x 6.8 cm with SUVmax 24.1, encasing the aorta and IVC without occlusion. This is borderline bulky by the >=10 cm criterion but is functionally bulky given the vascular encasement and mass effect (early satiety, epigastric/LUQ pain), and I am treating it as bulky disease for staging and treatment purposes.

Staging summary: stage IV, bulky, B-symptomatic DLBCL, NOS/GCB, ECOG 2, with 3 extranodal organs (renal, adrenal, hepatic), no marrow disease, no supra-diaphragmatic disease and no splenic disease. The indeterminate 4 mm right upper lobe nodule is below PET resolution and is staged as indeterminate, not as metastatic disease.
answer.biology:
GCB (Hans) subtype: CD10 positive, BCL6 positive, MUM1/IRF4 negative - the most favorable Hans category.

- Double-expressor status: NEGATIVE. MYC IHC 20% (<30-40%) and BCL2 IHC 30% (<50%); this is a deliberately important negative, because it means the IHC surrogates do not predict the aggressive biology of true double-expressor lymphoma.
- FISH: no MYC, BCL2 or BCL6 rearrangement (200 nuclei, adequate). Therefore not HGBL with MYC and/or BCL2 rearrangements, and not BCL6-rearranged high-grade B-cell lymphoma.
- Ki-67 approximately 70%: high, but below the >85-90% range typical of Burkitt lymphoma.
- EBER negative; no EBV-driven or EBV-positive DLBCL.
- CD5 negative, cyclin D1 negative, CD30 negative: excludes CLL/SLL, mantle cell, PMBCL and ALCL.
- Ki-67, BCL2 and MYC percentages are reported with approximate rounding and no scoring sheet or tumor-cell count; the FISH addendum is on block A1 only, so I will have the block re-reviewed for MYC/BCL2/BCL6 dual-fusion probes to exclude a masked rearrangement in a morphologically high-grade tumor.

Other biologic/prognostic markers: LDH 1,120 U/L on 2026-09-03 and rising to 1,290 on 2026-09-16 (ULN 225, roughly 5x ULN); beta-2 microglobulin 4.8 mg/L (ULN 2.2); albumin 3.1 g/dL; hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL; platelets 145 K; B2M and LDH both remain abnormal at baseline, which on this high-risk disease reinforces the need for careful interim assessment. Intended completion of the biologic workup: IG rearrangement FISH (IGH/IGK/IGL) plus IGHD clonality PCR and flow cytometry on the core biopsy, for final exclusion of high-grade B-cell lymphoma with 11q aberration and full immunophenotyping.
answer.prognosis:
High-risk DLBCL by every applicable index, with the highest-risk band in two of them.

- IPI = 5 of 5: age >60 (67), LDH elevated (~5x ULN), ECOG PS 2, stage III/IV, more than one extranodal site.
- NCCN-IPI = 5 of 5: albumin 3.1 (<3.5), LDH >1.5x ULN, age >60, stage III/IV, more than one extranodal site. This is the highest NCCN-IPI category (5-year OS approximately 30% in contemporary series).
- CNS-IPI = 6: age >60, elevated LDH, stage III/IV, more than one extranodal site, and kidney/adrenal involvement (weighted as 2 points). CNS-IPI 4-6 predicts a CNS relapse risk on the order of 10-15% without prophylaxis.

Adverse features beyond the indices: bulky 9.4 x 6.8 cm disease with aortic/IVC encasement and mechanical symptoms; three extranodal organs; B symptoms with 11% weight loss; albumin 3.1; B2M 4.8; anemia 9.9 with platelets 145; renal impairment (eGFR 50-55, creatinine rising 1.1 to 1.4 to 1.5 over 6 weeks, partly iatrogenic from NSAID use); ECOG 2; and comorbid diabetes with a steroid-unfriendly metabolic profile.

Favorable features: GCB subtype, no double-expressor/HGBL biology, no marrow involvement, no disease above the diaphragm, no splenic disease, preserved cardiac function (LVEF 60%, GLS -19%), no prior therapy, and a patient who is still fully independent in self-care and walking.

Expected outcome: with R-CHOP, 5-year overall survival for IPI 4-5 / NCCN-IPI 4-5 DLBCL in the rituximab era is roughly 30-40%, with 3-year PFS in the region of 45-55%. Cure remains possible and is his stated goal, but the honest framing for tumor board and for the patient is that the probability of cure is well under one-half, that relapse risk is concentrated in the CNS and in the bulky retroperitoneal site, and that treatment-related mortality is not negligible in a 67-year-old with ECOG 2, CKD stage 3a and hypoalbuminemia. A favorable Deauville 1-3 interim scan would raise the cure probability substantially; a Deauville 5 interim or end-of-treatment PET would lower it markedly.
answer.first_line_treatment:
R-CHOP-21 for 6 cycles (21-day cycles) with primary G-CSF support, CNS prophylaxis and tumor-lysis prophylaxis. Cycle 1 target date is the week of 2026-09-21 (before the wedding, which falls around cycle 5-6).

Regimen: rituximab 375 mg/m2 IV day 1; cyclophosphamide 750 mg/m2 IV day 1; doxorubicin 50 mg/m2 IV day 1; vincristine 1.4 mg/m2 IV day 1 (capped at 2 mg); prednisone 100 mg PO days 1-5. Pegfilgrastim 6 mg SC on day 2 of each cycle, with a CBC about 7-10 days after each nadir. Rituximab premedication: acetaminophen, antihistamine and corticosteroid for cycle 1, continued only for subsequent cycles if infusion reactions occur. Standard antiemetics (ondansetron plus dexamethasone) and a bowel regimen for vincristine-related constipation.

I am giving full CHOP doses despite his age, ECOG 2 and low albumin. Age, hypoalbuminemia and low performance status are not dose-reduction criteria in DLBCL, and dose attenuation is the most common avoidable cause of failure in high-risk disease. I will hold or reduce doses only for documented toxicity (febrile neutropenia, creatinine rise, neuropathy, hyperglycemia), and I will reassess dose intensity at each cycle. No chemotherapy dose adjustment is required for doxorubicin or vincristine at eGFR 50, and I will monitor closely for methotrexate-related renal clearance if HD-methotrexate is used.

What I am deliberately NOT doing, and why:
- Not R-CODOX-M/R-IVAC or R-CHOP-14: these are reserved for high-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC/BCL2 rearrangements and for PMBCL; in DLBCL NOS without rearrangements they add myelosuppression, mucositis, line complications and infection risk without a survival benefit. They also require infusional/inpatient nursing, which is a poor fit for a patient with ECOG 2 and a 45-minute drive.
- Not rituximab maintenance: no overall-survival benefit after R-CHOP in DLBCL (PRIMA-type maintenance data apply to indolent lymphoma).
- Not upfront autologous stem cell transplantation in first remission: standard only for high-grade B-cell lymphoma with MYC/BCL2 rearrangements; not indicated for DLBCL NOS.
- Not an anthracycline-sparing or reduced-intensity regimen at this time: LVEF is 60% with GLS -19%, and cure is his goal, so full-dose R-CHOP is the right trade-off.

Concurrent measures built into the plan: HD-methotrexate-based CNS prophylaxis (see cns_risk); allopurinol plus rasburicase with IV hydration and urine-output monitoring for tumor lysis (bulky disease, uric acid 10.4, rising creatinine, LDH ~5x ULN); an interim PET-CT after 3 cycles before cycle 4 to decide on intensification; end-of-treatment PET-CT; and consideration of consolidative involved-site radiotherapy to the bulky retroperitoneal site if a residual PET-avid mass persists (biopsy first). I will offer enrollment in a clinical trial for high-risk DLBCL at diagnosis and refer to a tertiary center if an appropriate trial is not available locally.

What would change this plan: (1) IG rearrangement or IGHD clonality studies, or hematopathology re-review, showing high-grade B-cell lymphoma with 11q aberration or an MYC-rearranged Burkitt-like lymphoma - I would move to intensified therapy (R-CHOP-14 or R-CODOX-M/R-IVAC-based) and plan autologous HSCT in first remission; (2) interim PET before cycle 4 showing Deauville 4 - I would continue the planned regimen and re-image after cycle 5; (3) interim PET showing Deauville 5 - I would biopsy the hottest site and, if active lymphoma is confirmed, intensify (dose-dense R-CHOP-14 with intrathecal CNS prophylaxis, or salvage R-DHAP/R-ICE x 2-3 with autologous transplant if this is progression); (4) frank progression before cycle 4 - salvage chemo (R-DHAP or R-ICE) x 2-3 then autologous transplant if chemosensitive, with CAR-T (axi-cel, liso-cel or relma-cel) in the relapse setting; (5) end-of-treatment PET-negative with a residual avid retroperitoneal mass - biopsy, and if active lymphoma, add involved-site radiotherapy; (6) MTX-related nephrotoxicity precluding systemic CNS prophylaxis - convert to intrathecal methotrexate/cytarabine; (7) ECOG decline to 3, or a serious new comorbidity - de-escalate to R-mini-CHOP or reduce cyclophosphamide/doxorubicin; (8) if he elects comfort-focused goals - symptom-directed therapy including palliative radiotherapy to the retroperitoneal mass instead of curative chemo.
answer.cns_risk:
HIGH, and I am treating this as a mandatory-prophylaxis patient.

CNS-IPI = 6 (highest band): age >60, LDH elevated, stage III/IV, more than one extranodal site, plus kidney and adrenal involvement (weighted 2 points). Supporting features: IPI 5/5 and NCCN-IPI 5/5, bulky high-SUV retroperitoneal disease, and three extranodal organs. Estimated CNS relapse risk without prophylaxis in this group is approximately 10-15%, and a CNS relapse is usually fatal and usually occurs within the first 2 years.

Important limitation of the workup to date: FDG PET is insensitive for intracranial disease (the report states this explicitly), so his normal brain uptake on PET does NOT exclude CNS involvement, and no brain imaging or CSF evaluation has been obtained. He is neurologically asymptomatic with a non-focal exam, so lumbar puncture is not required now (and I would not do a traumatic tap before confirming absence of a mass). I will obtain a baseline brain MRI with contrast before treatment to document the absence of occult CNS disease and to provide a comparison for any later symptom.

Prophylaxis plan (decision): systemic high-dose methotrexate, 3 g/m2 IV every 2 weeks for the first 3 cycles (or on day 15 of cycles 1-3), with 3 L/m2/day of IV hydration, urine alkalinization with sodium bicarbonate, and methotrexate level monitoring at 24, 48 and 72 hours - delayed clearance prompts leucovorin rescue, interruption of the methotrexate dose and re-dosing only once clearance is adequate. His eGFR of 50 permits 3 g/m2 provided I use nephrology-supported hydration; I will stop his ibuprofen now (it is both a renal insult and a counter-indication to methotrexate) and hold lisinopril around methotrexate days. Because his renal function is a moving target, I will add intrathecal methotrexate 12 mg plus cytarabine 50 mg on cycle day 1 (cycles 1-3, and cycle 4 if his kidneys do not allow systemic methotrexate to continue); if methotrexate clearance is delayed or renal function deteriorates further, intrathecal methotrexate/cytarabine becomes the primary route and I will not omit CNS prophylaxis because he is less than perfectly fit - doing so would convert a preventable, often fatal relapse pattern into a real one.

Additional CNS considerations: no CNS-directed radiotherapy is planned; I will monitor for methotrexate plus vincristine additive neurotoxicity (paresthesias, neuropathy) and for methotrexate neurotoxicity with each visit; MRI will be repeated if any headache, visual change, confusion, seizure, focal deficit or bladder/bowel change develops, and CSF cytology/flow will then be added (lumbar puncture only after imaging excludes a mass). I will advise that he report these symptoms immediately and that his NSAID use and headache self-treatment must be discussed with the team so that acetaminophen, not ibuprofen, is used.
answer.response_assessment:
Lugano 2014 criteria on the same modality used at baseline (FDG PET-CT), with Deauville scoring for the interim assessment. Both a complete and a partial response are defined by PET in this disease, and I will not use CT alone.

Interim PET-CT after 3 cycles (before cycle 4, approximately early December 2026): Deauville 1-3 = complete metabolic response - complete the remaining 3 cycles of R-CHOP as planned with no change. Deauville 4 = partial metabolic response - continue the planned regimen unchanged (I do not intensify on Deauville 4 alone) and repeat PET after cycle 5. Deauville 5 = positive - biopsy the highest-SUV lesion before acting, because post-chemotherapy inflammation in the retroperitoneum is a frequent false positive; if active lymphoma is confirmed I will intensify, and if this represents progression I will move to salvage R-DHAP/R-ICE x 2-3 with autologous stem cell transplantation if chemosensitive.

End-of-treatment PET-CT 8-12 weeks after the last cycle (timing chosen so that treatment-related inflammation has resolved, to reduce false positives): a complete metabolic response requires Deauville 1-3 with no new lesion and no new disease elsewhere. A residual avid mass at the primary site will be biopsied before I escalate therapy or add radiotherapy, since fibrosis, inflammation and post-treatment change can remain FDG-avid. Any new or enlarging avid lesion at end of treatment is progression and triggers the salvage pathway (R-DHAP/R-ICE x 2-3 then autologous transplant; CAR-T for relapse after transplant).

Concurrently at each visit: serum LDH (1,290 and rising on 2026-09-16; normalization is a supportive adjunct, not a response criterion), CBC with differential and CMP with potassium, phosphate, calcium, creatinine and urate before each cycle for tumor-lysis surveillance, weight, ECOG performance status, neuropathy assessment on vincristine, and a focused neurologic examination.

Specific imaging follow-up decisions: the incidental 4 mm right upper lobe nodule is below the resolution of PET and cannot be characterized by the staging study; I will obtain a dedicated thin-section diagnostic chest CT at approximately 3 months (after cycle 2) and again at 6-12 months, with biopsy if it enlarges or becomes avid. This does not change current management (he is already stage IV) but it must not be lost. No routine surveillance imaging is indicated after a complete metabolic response - clinical assessment and laboratory monitoring every 3 months for 2 years, then every 6 months to 5 years, plus the chest CT protocol above for the nodule. CNS restaging is not planned in the asymptomatic patient; brain MRI is the surveillance tool if symptoms arise.
answer.pretreatment_workup:
Already completed and adequate: CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast 2026-08-15; FDG PET-CT skull base to mid-thigh 2026-09-05 (technically good - mediastinal blood pool SUVmax 2.1, liver 2.9, glucose 142 at injection); CT-guided core biopsy of the retroperitoneal mass with full immunohistochemistry and FISH addendum 2026-09-12/2026-09-16; right posterior iliac crest aspirate and biopsy with flow cytometry, negative for lymphoma, 2026-09-13; CBC with differential, CMP, LDH, uric acid, beta-2 microglobulin, calcium, albumin, HbA1c on 2026-09-03 with repeat chemistries on 2026-09-16; transthoracic echocardiogram 2026-09-09 (LVEF 60%, GLS -19%, no effusion, grade I diastolic dysfunction); hepatitis B surface antigen negative, total core antibody negative, surface antibody reactive (immune from vaccination - no antiviral prophylaxis and no HBV DNA monitoring required), hepatitis C antibody negative, HIV 1/2 negative on 2026-09-03.

Outstanding before cycle 1, with reasons:
- 12-lead ECG with QTc: no ECG on file; needed before vincristine, ondansetron and doxorubicin and as a baseline for QT and ST assessment.
- Brain MRI with contrast: PET cannot evaluate the brain and his CNS-IPI is 6; establishes a baseline and rules out occult CNS disease before intrathecal therapy is ever needed.
- Quantitative immunoglobulins (IgG, IgA, IgM): baseline before anti-CD20 to identify hypogammaglobulinemia, which is plausible with hypoalbuminemia and malnutrition, and to define immunoglobulin replacement thresholds.
- G6PD level: required before rasburicase.
- Urinalysis, urine pH and baseline weight and 24-hour urine output: tumor-lysis monitoring baseline.
- Iron studies (ferritin, iron, transferrin saturation) and consideration of GI evaluation: hemoglobin 9.9 with MCV 86 plus four weeks of ibuprofen 1600 mg/day plus 11% weight loss; both lymphoma and NSAID-related ulcer bleeding are plausible, and I need the iron studies before I attribute the anemia entirely to lymphoma.
- Diabetes management plan for steroid-induced hyperglycemia: glucose 168, HbA1c 7.4%, on metformin; I will increase monitoring, anticipate insulin requirement during prednisone days and hold metformin if renal function falls further or if contrast is required.
- Vaccination: confirm and update influenza, pneumococcal (PCV20) and COVID-19 vaccines before or at cycle 1; no live vaccines during or after therapy; household contacts should be vaccinated.
- Formal geriatric/frailty and nutrition assessment with dietitian: ECOG 2, albumin 3.1, 11% weight loss, early satiety; this directly determines supportive intensity and my decisions about dose reduction if his status declines.
- Nephrology input: CKD stage 3a with a creatinine rising from 1.1 (2025-07-14) to 1.4 to 1.5, and HD-methotrexate dosing and hydration will require coordination.
- Cardiac monitoring plan: baseline echo is adequate for doxorubicin (LVEF 60%, GLS -19% at the lower limit of normal); repeat echo with GLS after cycle 3 rather than waiting until the end, track cumulative doxorubicin to 300 mg/m2, and switch to MUGA if GLS falls.
- Vascular access plan: peripheral IV with a weekly or biweekly oncology nurse visit is preferred over a PICC or port, given 6 cycles and the thrombotic and infection risk of central access (and no benefit for repeated marrow checks since the marrow is uninvolved).
- Final biologic completion: IG (IGH/IGK/IGL) rearrangement FISH, IGHD clonality PCR and flow cytometry on the core, with hematopathology re-review; dual-fusion FISH if the block review raises doubt.
- Not required and explicitly not ordered: pregnancy testing (male patient), fertility preservation (age 67), CSF cytology and flow (no neurologic symptoms; no lumbar puncture without prior imaging), and routine CT surveillance after complete response.
- Management item I will handle today: stop ibuprofen 400 mg three to four times daily (nephrotoxicity with rising creatinine, bleeding risk with prednisone and anticipated thrombocytopenia, and it is a contraindication to methotrexate and a risk amplifier for tumor lysis); substitute acetaminophen at up to 3 g/day given the alkaline phosphatase of 168, and treat his gout with allopurinol (which serves both the tumor-lysis prophylaxis and his gout) rather than NSAIDs.
answer.supportive_care:
Tumor lysis syndrome prevention (mandatory, given bulky disease, uric acid 10.4 rising from 9.8, LDH ~5x ULN, phosphate 4.6 and potassium 5.0): start allopurinol 300 mg daily (renally adjusted and titrated) about 5 days before cycle 1 and target a uric acid below 6.0; rasburicase 3.6 mg IV fixed dose on day 0 or day 1 (after checking G6PD, and repeat dosing only for rising uric acid); IV hydration 2.5-3 L/m2/day with urine output maintained above 100 mL/hour; monitor potassium, phosphate, calcium, creatinine, uric acid and urine output every 12 hours for the first 2-3 days and then daily for each cycle; furosemide only if needed to maintain output; do NOT alkalinize the urine while using rasburicase (precipitates rasburicase and risks xanthine nephropathy) - I will coordinate alkalinization strictly with the methotrexate days. His low-grade fever and tachypnea-free lungs are reassuring but I will watch for the early pattern of hyperkalemia, hypocalcemia with tetany and rising creatinine.

Neutropenia: primary G-CSF with every cycle (pegfilgrastim 6 mg on day 2). Fever threshold 38.0 C with an immediate call rule, and no NSAID self-treatment at fever because steroids mask the temperature and NSAIDs are renally toxic. CBC about 7-10 days after each pegfilgrastim nadir, and I will hold cycles for ANC below 500 or platelets below 50 K.

Infection prophylaxis: Pneumocystis prophylaxis with atovaquone 1500 mg PO daily (I am avoiding trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole given his sulfonamide antibiotic allergy with maculopapular rash in 2009; dapsone is a reasonable alternative if G6PD is normal). Herpesvirus prophylaxis with valacyclovir 500 mg BID during neutropenia or with significant mucositis. Antifungal: fluconazole during neutropenia if mucositis develops - and specifically I will avoid voriconazole and other strong CYP3A4 inhibitors because of marked vincristine neurotoxicity with azole-vincristine combinations. Rituximab infusion reactions premedicated; no live vaccines; influenza, pneumococcal and COVID-19 vaccines given before or at cycle 1.

Renal protection: stop ibuprofen; avoid nephrotoxins and minimize IV contrast; hold lisinopril around methotrexate days and during any acute illness with AKI; nephrology input for methotrexate dosing; do not force hydration beyond what his CKD tolerates without monitoring; avoid aminoglycosides.

Cardiac: baseline LVEF 60% with GLS -19%, repeat echocardiogram with GLS after cycle 3 and at end of treatment, cumulative doxorubicin tracked to 300 mg/m2, tight BP control (continue lisinopril when renal function allows), continue atorvastatin 40 mg (also appropriate for his hyperlipidemia and cardiovascular risk) - note that rifampin is not used, so no statin interaction with rituximab is expected.

Metabolic: prednisone will drive hyperglycemia - home glucose monitoring, proactive insulin (or metformin adjustment) rather than waiting for symptomatic hyperglycemia; monitor for steroid myopathy and proximal weakness against the background of doxorubicin and vincristine neuropathy, with a rehabilitation assessment if symptoms appear; monitor for hyperglycemia and adrenal suppression with 5-day bursts (short courses, so adrenal suppression is unlikely, but I will give a stress-dose plan if he becomes febrile and septic).

Gout: no urate-lowering therapy was in place; allopurinol started for tumor lysis will also cover his gout, and I will titrate to a uric acid below 6.0 with renal dose adjustment. For flares during chemotherapy I will use short corticosteroid bursts or low-dose colchicine, with colchicine used at a reduced dose and caution, because colchicine plus atorvastatin plus renal impairment risks myopathy, and it also interacts with CYP3A4-metabolized drugs. NSAIDs are excluded.

Symptom and nutrition: dietitian referral for 11% weight loss, albumin 3.1 and early satiety (high-calorie oral supplements, small frequent meals, consider ondansetron for early satiety and nausea); analgesia with acetaminophen rather than NSAIDs; monitor for obstruction complications of the encasing mass (urinary obstruction, hydronephrosis, gastric outlet obstruction, vascular thrombosis) and involve urology and interventional radiology early if the renal function continues to deteriorate or if venous thrombosis of the renal or iliac veins develops; GI upset from cyclophosphamide and doxorubicin with scheduled ondansetron and dexamethasone; constipation prophylaxis with senna or polyethylene glycol plus vincristine, with monitoring for ileus; monitor for vincristine peripheral and autonomic neuropathy with grip strength and reflexes, and hold or reduce vincristine for grade 3 neuropathy; ensure the 45-minute drive is not a barrier (see fitness_and_goals).

Practical and safety: chemotherapy and infusions in a setting with vitals monitoring and resuscitation capability (to cover anaphylaxis risk with rituximab and to manage any infusion reaction); premedication protocol documented; no blood products unless needed; no central line; keep the NSAID discontinuation and the sulfamide allergy flagged in the chart and pharmacy order set; a written tumor-lysis and neutropenic-emergency plan for the patient and family.

Follow-up after completion: history, examination, CBC and chemistries every 3 months for 2 years, then every 6 months to 5 years, with the dedicated chest CT protocol for the 4 mm lung nodule; no routine PET or CT in complete remission; late effects monitored (cardiac, endocrine, neuropathy, secondary malignancy); and a low threshold for imaging if any new B symptom or focal sign appears.
answer.fitness_and_goals:
Functionally he is ECOG 2 (documented 2026-09-02; still independent in self-care and ambulates, but rests most afternoons) with 11% unintentional weight loss (79 to 70.2 kg), albumin 3.1 g/dL and hemoglobin 9.9 g/dL. He is not frail in the classic sense - he has no prior cancer therapy, no known heart disease, an LVEF of 60% with preserved global function, and no functional decline in his basic activities - but he has a reduced physiologic reserve (ECOG 2, hypoalbuminemia, CKD stage 3a with a creatinine still climbing, uncontrolled diabetes with glucose 168 and HbA1c 7.4%).

Comorbidity management and fitness: the two comorbidities that will actually constrain therapy are renal function and steroid-induced hyperglycemia; both are addressable (stopping the NSAID should improve the creatinine, and steroid-related glucose can be managed with insulin and tighter monitoring). The gout is not a barrier once allopurinol is on board. I judge him fit for full-dose R-CHOP with G-CSF support, and I would rather give full-dose therapy with careful monitoring than pre-emptively reduce him to R-mini-CHOP, because under-dosing is the clearest preventable cause of failure in high-risk DLBCL. I will complete a formal geriatric/frailty assessment and a nutrition assessment before cycle 1 so that this decision is documented rather than assumed, and I will re-derive it at each cycle: if ECOG drifts to 3 or he sustains a serious infection or renal deterioration, I will de-escalate (R-mini-CHOP or reduced cyclophosphamide/doxorubicin) and refocus the discussion on disease control.

Goals of care, as stated by him at the 2026-09-17 visit and to be confirmed with him and his family: he wants treatment aimed at cure, not palliation. He wants to attend his granddaughter's mid-December wedding. He is concerned about the 45-minute drive for frequent visits. He has a wife who drives and a daughter living nearby, and both were present for the results discussion.

How the plan serves those goals: with cycles starting the week of 2026-09-21, cycles 1-4 fall before mid-December and cycle 5-6 straddle it. He will most likely be between cycles with a partial or near-complete response at the wedding, and I will schedule the interim PET after cycle 3 (early December) so that any change in plan is known before the wedding rather than after it. I will schedule pre-medications and growth factor to minimize fatigue in the days around the wedding (avoid day 1-2 and the nadir in the week before), and I will aim for the nadir to fall after rather than before the event. I will also be honest at tumor board and with him that a bulky stage IV high-grade B-cell lymphoma is unlikely to be in complete metabolic response by mid-December, so the realistic goal for December is control of disease with preserved function - which is what matters for the wedding - and that the goal he has chosen (cure) carries a probability of well under one-half.

Logistics and shared decision-making: chemo and labs will be delivered close to home with only the necessary visits at the cancer center (a standard G-CSF regimen needs roughly 2 visits per cycle plus a nadir blood draw), I will consolidate the echo, blood draws and PET into single trips, I will assess whether local infusion can be arranged for cycles 4-6, and I will avoid regimens requiring continuous infusion or inpatient care (R-CODOX-M/R-IVAC) partly for this reason. I will document informed consent including the specific risks of high-dose methotrexate CNS prophylaxis and its renal requirement, the risk of neutropenic sepsis and tumor lysis, the risk of anthracycline cardiotoxicity and neuropathy, the infertility/fertility implications (not relevant at his age), the rare risk of secondary malignancy, and the possibility that his disease relapses. I will revisit the goals of care and advance-care planning at each response assessment, and I will offer a palliative-care co-management referral now for symptom control (pain, early satiety, fatigue) rather than waiting for the end of the line.
